lesson.title: Citizenship and Equal Protection: The Fourteenth Amendment
lesson.summary: Ratified in 1868 largely in response to the Black Codes, the Fourteenth Amendment made all persons born in the United States citizens and guaranteed equal protection of the law, reshaping the relationship between individuals and the federal government.
lesson.body:
By the end of 1865, the Thirteenth Amendment had abolished slavery, but it said nothing about what rights the roughly four million newly freed people actually possessed. Southern state legislatures answered that question themselves, passing Black Codes that restricted freedpeople's ability to own property, choose employers, move freely, or testify against white people in court. President Andrew Johnson, who had taken office after Lincoln's assassination, did little to stop these laws and in fact vetoed a federal Civil Rights Act intended to counter them. Congress overrode his veto in April 1866, but Republican lawmakers worried that a simple statute could be repealed by a future Congress or struck down by hostile courts. They wanted the protections written permanently into the Constitution, and the result was the Fourteenth Amendment.

The amendment's first section did the most sweeping work. It declared that all persons born or naturalized in the United States, and subject to its jurisdiction, are citizens of the United States and of the state where they reside. This directly overturned the Supreme Court's 1857 decision in Dred Scott v. Sandford, which had held that Black Americans could never be citizens. The same section barred states from depriving any person of life, liberty, or property without due process of law, and from denying any person within their jurisdiction the equal protection of the laws. These due process and equal protection clauses would become, over the following century, the constitutional basis for nearly every major civil rights ruling in American history, from school desegregation to countless later cases.

The amendment also carried three lesser known but politically important provisions. Section 2 reduced a state's representation in Congress if it denied the vote to adult male citizens, a mechanism meant to pressure Southern states into extending suffrage to Black men. Section 3 barred former Confederate officials who had previously sworn an oath to the Constitution from holding federal or state office, unless Congress voted to remove that disability. Section 4 declared the Confederate war debt void and affirmed that the United States debt was valid, closing off any possibility of former Confederates seeking compensation for emancipated slaves or war losses.

Congress passed the amendment in June 1866, but ratification became entangled with the broader fight over Reconstruction. When most former Confederate states refused to ratify it, Congress made ratification a requirement for readmission to the Union under the Reconstruction Act of 1867, forcing Southern states to accept it as a condition of restoring their representation in Congress. The amendment was finally declared ratified on July 9, 1868, a milestone that marked the beginning of the more assertive phase of Congressional, or Radical, Reconstruction.

Despite its sweeping language, the Fourteenth Amendment's promises went largely unenforced in the South for nearly a century after ratification. State and local governments found ways around it, and federal courts often interpreted it narrowly. Its true power would not be realized until the civil rights movement of the twentieth century, but its text remained on the books throughout, waiting to be enforced.
